claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 typically contains residual porosity and microstructural flaws.
Residual porosity and microstructural flaws promote hole formation during exposure to a liquid plating bath.
ZrB2 specimens can be fabricated using an SPS route.
SPS at 1850–1950 °C for 10–20 minutes under at least 40 MPa can produce fully dense, single-phase ZrB2.
The proposed SPS treatment produces fewer internal pores than conventional high-temperature sintering.
Reducing internal pores will reduce hole formation and subsequent component failure during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
The proposed preparation window is SPS at 1850–1950 °C with a 10–20 minute dwell, pulsed direct current, at least 40 MPa pressure, and an inert atmosphere.
Rapid SPS consolidation and limited grain growth enhance densification and minimize intergranular pores and microstructural defects.
Pulsed electric current and pressure accelerate mass transport and diffusion in ZrB2 at lower temperatures.
Accelerated mass transport produces faster densification and reduces the opportunity for pore coarsening.
Rapid SPS processing minimizes thermal gradients that otherwise cause defects in conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have higher density and fewer residual pores than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Higher density and fewer pores will improve resistance to liquid infiltration.
Improved resistance to liquid infiltration will reduce component failure during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
Conventional ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C shows significant porosity and degradation under long-term liquid plating conditions.
The service boundary is prolonged exposure to a representative liquid plating bath at typical operational temperatures and durations.
